cases.title: Vinh Loc B Resettlement Quarter, Ho Chi Minh City
cases.place: Vinh Loc B, Binh Chanh district, Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are the administrative centre of the Vinh Loc area on the western edge of Ho Chi Minh City, where the project's Vinh Loc B resettlement quarter was built. The canal and street works that displaced the households are about 12 to 20 km away in the inner city.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit C3887-VN of SDR 148.8 million (about US$222.5 million) for the Vietnam Urban Upgrading Project, approved 29 April 2004, effective 6 October 2004. Additional financing Credit 4604-VN of US$160 million was approved in September 2009, most of it for the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal works in Ho Chi Minh City. The project closed on 31 December 2014, two years later than planned. A Japanese PHRD grant (TF-53182) of US$4.839 million was also used. Compensation and resettlement cost US$188.5 million against US$111.3 million estimated at appraisal.

lenders.name: Agence Française de Développement
lenders.role: Expected at appraisal to lend about US$37.5 million towards the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal basin works. The World Bank's completion report says that in 2005 it became clear AFD could not provide the money, and the gap was covered by the Bank's additional financing instead.

cases.conditions: The project's resettlement plans required that everyone adversely affected, people without land papers included, be paid for their losses at replacement cost and be helped to keep the living standards and earning capacity they had before construction started (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2015).
cases.community: The project upgraded low-income areas in Ho Chi Minh City, Hai Phong, Nam Dinh and Can Tho. Its largest single work was the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal in Ho Chi Minh City, which runs through a densely built part of the city. The World Bank's completion report records 2,917 households permanently relocated and 18,959 households partly affected, against 4,859 and 16,569 estimated at appraisal. For Ho Chi Minh City the resettlement site was Vinh Loc B in Binh Chanh district, 30.6 hectares, where the project built 529 land plots and 1,939 apartments. Across the four cities the project built 2,641 plots and 2,383 apartments, of which 2,547 were used to rehouse people displaced by the project.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report rates compliance with all four safeguard policies satisfactory, and says independent monitoring consultants found most affected households kept or improved their pre-project living standards. The same report records substantial delays in organising resettlement and in paying compensation, and gives three reasons: checking which households were legally eligible took longer than expected, some households would only move or take payment on dates they considered auspicious, and government cost norms were out of date so payments had to be revised repeatedly as land prices rose. The Independent Evaluation Group's 2016 review states that resettlement and compensation to households suffered severe delays and that delays in counterpart funds for land acquisition and compensation made resettlement take longer than planned. Of 571 complaints collected by the project's grievance system, 568 were resolved by closing; three in Nam Dinh were still open and were passed to city-funded projects. Ten years after the loan closed, VietNamNet reported on 26 June 2024 that about 1,500 apartments at Vinh Loc B stood empty, that the quarter is about 20 km from the city centre, and quoted a resident, Tran Thi Hong, who moved in during 2016 after losing land to a canal project: her apartment was roomier but her income from selling bread fell by half from VND 12 million a month, only 10 of 60 apartments near her were occupied when she arrived, and some families left within months because they could not find work. Another resident who moved in during 2018, Nguyen Thi Hoa, described mould on walls, peeling paint and cracked interior walls. VnExpress reported in 2024 that Vinh Loc B has 1,900 apartments, 80 percent of them unoccupied, that the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Construction counts the quarter as nearly a quarter of the city's roughly 9,000 vacant resettlement units, and quoted Tran Huu Son, who gave up land for the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal project in 2012 and took cash rather than an apartment 12 km from his old home, although the cash was not enough to buy a new one.

cases.title: Bac Son-Nam Hai Road, Haiphong: Resettlement Held Up for Years
cases.place: Bac Son to Nam Hai east-west road link, Haiphong, Viet Nam
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are the midpoint of the Bac Son-Nam Hai east-west road link, which runs across Haiphong from Bac Son in An Duong to Nam Hai in Hai An.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49000 of US$175 million for the Haiphong Urban Transport Project, approved 29 March 2011, effective 28 July 2011, closed 29 February 2020 after the closing date was moved three years and two months from 31 December 2016. US$152.5 million was disbursed. The Haiphong city government was to put in US$101.61 million, including compensation, resettlement and livelihood restoration for affected people and the building of resettlement sites.

cases.conditions: The project's resettlement policy framework, prepared under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, was approved by the prime minister's office; two resettlement action plans were agreed with the Bank and approved by the Haiphong City People's Committee (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2020).
cases.community: The project surveyed 3,037 affected households in 13 communes and wards of Haiphong for the new road. It identified 909 households that had to be moved. Acquiring the land for the resettlement sites themselves affected a further 871 households, 4,223 people.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says land acquisition and resettlement were the main reason the project ran late, and names the cause: the Haiphong government's financial constraints in providing its share of the money, and delays in handing sites to contractors. At the mid-term review in October 2014 the Bank identified inadequate counterpart funding as a cause of delay; one stretch of delay ran to nearly eight months, and the project was restructured to move savings into three resettlement site contracts. Delays continued through the last three years, which the report attributes to persisting difficulties in resettlement and to insufficient money in the city's 2016-2020 medium-term investment plan. By November 2018, less than 18 months before closing, 69 resettlement cases were still unresolved, about 6 percent of the 3,037 cases. Completion of the road component ran nearly 3.5 years late, and the report says more than 80 percent of that delay is attributable to those remaining 6 percent of cases. Implementation progress was rated moderately unsatisfactory in nine of the project's 20 progress reports. By October 2019, 109 cases (3.5 percent) had been resolved and three were open; one was still open when the project closed in February 2020 and is recorded as resolved on 1 October 2020. The road opened on 3 May 2020.

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework complying with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 was prepared by the government and cleared by the Bank before appraisal, and applied to every subproject for the life of the project; sub-project resettlement plans had to be cleared by the Bank before works began (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2017).
cases.community: Two first-phase resettlement plans counted 7,245 displaced people on the waterways and 2,840 on the national highways and provincial roads. By the end of the project the number of affected households had risen from 15,000 to 22,663, an increase of over 30 percent, on 518.43 hectares of land. The completion report says the majority were only marginally affected, losing trees, garden fences and similar. Its annex lists the households province by province: 3,638 on the road component, 7,620 on the waterway component and 11,405 on the provincial roads component, in Tra Vinh, Can Tho, An Giang, Dong Thap, Kien Giang, Tien Giang, Soc Trang, Bac Lieu, Long An, Ca Mau and Ho Chi Minh City.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says there was general compliance with the resettlement policy framework, and that in the early years there were a small number of cases in which affected people were not compensated in accordance with the approved safeguards measures, which the implementing units addressed. At the closing date of 30 June 2016, compensation had not been completed for about 110 households on the waterway component because of a dispute over the compensation rate. The government undertook to carry on paying under the project's resettlement framework with monthly Bank monitoring; when the report was written in January 2017, 30 households were still waiting, with payment planned by the end of March 2017. The report also records that insufficient counterpart money for compensation was a barrier throughout: contractors could not always reach construction sites because resettlement claims were unresolved, provinces advanced their own budgets to pay people and claimed the money back later, delays pushed compensation costs up, and in late 2015 an unforeseen US$52 million more in counterpart funds was called for to cover additional resettlement costs.

cases.title: Urban Water and Wastewater Project: Structures Paid at Part of Replacement Value

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA and IBRD)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49480 of US$200 million for the Urban Water Supply and Wastewater Project, approved 24 May 2011, effective 7 October 2011, closed 31 December 2019. Additional financing of US$69 million (IBRD-86210) and US$50 million (IDA-58170) was added in May 2016 for a wastewater and drainage subproject in Di An. Total Bank financing disbursed was US$266.5 million of a US$299.6 million project.

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework and 15 resettlement action plans were prepared and disclosed in December 2010 under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12. The Bank's completion report states that compensation levels and assistance were to be set at replacement cost and to account for living standards and earning capacity before the project (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2020).
cases.community: The project built water supply, wastewater and drainage works in Di An and My Phuoc (Binh Duong), Dong Xoai (Binh Phuoc), Phu Quoc (Kien Giang), Da Lat (Lam Dong), Thai Hoa (Nghe An), Ninh Binh, Tam Ky (Quang Nam), Uong Bi (Quang Ninh), Dong Ha (Quang Tri) and Bim Son (Thanh Hoa). At appraisal 870,583 square metres of land were to be taken and 556 households affected, 9 of them moved. During implementation 3,081 households were affected: 45 had to be moved, 455 lost more than 20 percent of their farmland, and 2,581 were marginally affected through partial loss of farm or residential land, of secondary structures, or for the duration of construction.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says all compensation to households was completed and that at closing there were no grievances or outstanding issues, and that independent monitoring surveys found most affected households kept or improved their pre-project living standards. In the same passage it records that local authorities often applied government rules where gaps were found in compensation plans, including the assistance given to households that lost 30 percent of their farmland, and compensation for structures on agricultural land at 50 to 80 percent of replacement value. Provincial project units and local authorities were asked to settle those issues during implementation. The report states that by the end of the project the issues had been addressed in most subprojects, except in the Thai Hoa and Ninh Binh subprojects, where the status had not been officially confirmed to the World Bank. The report also records that land acquisition documentation was not adequately prepared in some subprojects, and that in Di An preparing a cadastral map and identifying landowners took more than a year.

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plans were prepared and accepted by the Bank under its involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, and resettlement plans had to be in place before civil works began on each subproject (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2018).
cases.community: The project built irrigation, drainage and salinity-control works, rural water supply and bridges in seven Mekong Delta provinces, among them An Giang, Bac Lieu, Ca Mau, Can Tho, Hau Giang and Soc Trang. The Bank's completion report records 5,435 households affected: 215 had to move, 304 lost part of their farmland and 70 had to rebuild their house on the land they had left.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says the project faced a significant number of resettlement problems, and lists the causes: disputes over land title, the rates of compensation, differences between the Vietnamese government's resettlement rules and the Bank's, and late payment of resettlement compensation because counterpart money was not available. There were 260 resettlement-related grievances, 250 of them settled by the provincial project units themselves. The report says that by project completion all grievances and outstanding issues had been settled by local authorities and the project units, that everyone adversely affected including informal settlers was paid at replacement cost, and that independent monitoring consultants found affected households kept or improved their pre-project living standards. The Independent Evaluation Group's 2018 review of the report repeats that resettlement documents were prepared and accepted and gives no figures of its own.

dropped.reason: Dropped: ICIJ's 773,838 is not a count of people moved. Opened the World Bank's Project Appraisal Document (21 October 2004), the Integrated Safeguards Data Sheet (24 May 2004), the 2009 additional financing project paper, the 13 December 2014 Implementation Completion and Results Report and the Independent Evaluation Group's 12 May 2015 review of it, all read from disk as text. The ISDS states: 'The Project will not involve any major resettlement', 'In the first phase of project 131,955 households will be affected by the Project. The number of DPs is high because of the DPs are scattered along the lines', 'Most of impacts on land will be temporary', and 'Impacts on houses will be mostly partial and generally will not require the relocation of families outside their residential plots.' The PAD's Annex 13 classifies impacts in seven categories, five of them temporary right-of-way impacts, and its table for the six Phase 1(a) provinces gives 178 families losing more than 10 percent of their productive land, 299,746 square metres of permanent acquisition and 14,256,140 square metres of temporary acquisition. The completion report says 'The negative impacts of project activities are generally minor because most of the lines were rehabilitated from the existing ones. A small volume of land acquisition was required for the new alignments and substations', records difficulties in land acquisition in some provinces, and rates overall compliance with social safeguard policies satisfactory; the IEG review repeats this. No document opened gives the figure 773,838 or any figure for people physically moved, and no documented failure was found. The figure appears to be a count of project-affected persons in the widest sense, consistent with ICIJ's published method of counting 'project-affected people' and including temporary impacts.

Dropped: a 13-province distribution network with no identified community and no documented failure finding. Opened the 24 December 2013 Implementation Completion and Results Report (read from disk as text). It says the project 'caused modest land acquisition for the individual project affected household and small community-wide socioeconomic impacts', that many subprojects used existing rights of way, and that 'The land acquisition and compensation activities by Implementation Agencies satisfactorily complied with OP 4.12'. It lists challenges including disagreements by affected households with proposed compensation rates. One finding worth recording: in the borrower's own completion report, annexed to the ICR, Central Power Corporation writes that 'Compensation unit price in provinces was low as compared with average price of the market, interfering significantly in compensation declaration to local residents' and that 'people did not accept compensation, obstructed construction and made long solving time'. That is the implementing company's self-report, names no place and gives no number of households, so it does not carry a case on its own.

Dropped: the actual displacement was small and no failure is documented.
